lead: AWS's most popular cert. It proves you can design systems on AWS that are secure, keep running when parts fail, perform well and don't waste money, following the Well-Architected Framework. Expect long scenarios where two answers would work and you pick the one that best fits what's asked: lowest cost, least effort or highest availability.
objSub: Four domains and 14 task statements from AWS's SAA-C03 exam guide. Tick them off as you study; progress saves on this device.

c03.label: C03
c03.note: The only version on sale. AWS hasn't announced an SAA-C04. AWS refreshed the exam guide's service lists in 2026 (latest Oct 29, 2026), and changes reach the exam about a month after they're posted, so study from the current guide.
c03.onote: Official AWS task statements (SAA-C03 exam guide), in plain words. Weights are AWS's share of scored content.

domains.name: Design Secure Architectures
obj: Secure access to AWS resources

IAM users, groups, roles and policies; least privilege; MFA and root protection; IAM Identity Center and federation; cross-account roles; AWS Organizations with service control policies (SCPs); temporary credentials from STS.
Secure workloads and applications

VPC design with public and private subnets; security groups and network ACLs; WAF, Shield and GuardDuty; Cognito for app sign-in; Secrets Manager; VPN and Direct Connect; VPC endpoints to keep traffic off the internet.
Data security controls
Encryption at rest and in transit with KMS and ACM; key rotation; S3 bucket policies, Block Public Access and Object Lock; backup and retention; finding sensitive data with Macie.

domains.name: Design Resilient Architectures
obj: Scalable and loosely coupled architectures
Decouple tiers with SQS, SNS and EventBridge; API Gateway; serverless with Lambda and Fargate; containers; Auto Scaling; caching; stateless designs; Step Functions workflows.
Highly available and fault-tolerant architectures

Multi-AZ and multi-Region designs; load balancers; Route 53 health checks and failover; RDS Multi-AZ and read replicas; disaster recovery strategies chosen by RTO and RPO; no single points of failure.

domains.name: Design High-Performing Architectures
obj: High-performing storage
S3, EBS volume types, EFS and FSx; picking by access pattern, throughput and IOPS; S3 Transfer Acceleration and multipart upload.
High-performing and elastic compute
EC2 instance families and sizes, Auto Scaling, Lambda, containers on ECS and EKS, Fargate; decoupling so each tier scales on its own.
High-performing databases
RDS vs Aurora vs DynamoDB; read replicas; RDS Proxy; caching with ElastiCache and DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX); picking the engine and capacity.
High-performing networks
CloudFront and Global Accelerator; VPC subnets and routing; Transit Gateway, VPC peering and PrivateLink; load balancer types; Direct Connect and VPN.
Data ingestion and transformation
Streaming with Kinesis; ETL with Glue; querying S3 with Athena; data lakes with Lake Formation; moving data with DataSync and the Snow Family; dashboards with QuickSight.

domains.name: Design Cost-Optimized Architectures
obj: Cost-optimized storage
S3 storage classes, lifecycle rules and Intelligent-Tiering; right-sized EBS volumes; backup retention; tracking with Cost Explorer and Budgets.
Cost-optimized compute
On-Demand vs Savings Plans vs Reserved vs Spot; right-sizing; Graviton instances; Auto Scaling to match demand; Lambda for spiky loads.
Cost-optimized databases
Right-size DB instances; Aurora Serverless and DynamoDB on-demand for unpredictable loads; reserved DB capacity; snapshot and backup retention costs.
Cost-optimized networks
Data transfer between AZs, Regions and the internet; NAT gateway costs vs free gateway endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB; CloudFront to cut origin traffic; Direct Connect vs VPN.

A disk for EC2, in one AZ

Data replicated live; servers off until needed

rows: Holds messages until a worker pulls them; absorbs spikes
Pushes one message to many subscribers
Routes events by rules, from AWS and SaaS apps

HTTP/HTTPS; route by path or host name
TCP/UDP; very high volume; static IPs

method: Use the four domains above. Security is the biggest at 30%, and it shows up inside the other domains too.
One full video course, start to finish. Then read AWS's Well-Architected pillar summaries and the disaster recovery whitepaper.
In a personal Free Tier account: a VPC with public and private subnets, an ALB with Auto Scaling, an RDS Multi-AZ database, an S3 bucket with a lifecycle rule. Tear it down after.
Flashcards for the clue table, storage types, DR strategies and pricing models.
Timed practice exams. For every miss, write down why each wrong answer was wrong, not just why the right one was right.
tips: Underline the deciding words: “most cost-effective,” “least operational overhead,” “highly available.” They decide between two answers that both work.
If one answer runs a database on EC2 and another uses RDS, the managed one usually wins unless the question needs OS access.
130 minutes for 65 long questions is about two minutes each. Flag the long ones and come back.
Cross off answers that break a rule first: public buckets, long-lived keys, single AZ. It's often down to two after that.

quiz.q: Auditors in Account B need read-only access to CloudTrail logs in an S3 bucket in Account A. What's the MOST secure way?
o: Create a role in Account A with read-only access to the bucket and a trust policy for Account B; auditors assume it
Right. Cross-account roles give temporary credentials and keep permissions in one place.
Add a bucket policy that gives Account B's root principal s3:* on the bucket
It works, but s3:* lets them delete and change logs. That's far from read-only.
Create IAM users in Account A with access keys for each auditor
It works, but long-lived keys and extra users are more to protect and manage.
Attach an SCP in Organizations that allows Account B to read the bucket
SCPs never grant access. They only set the maximum an account can be allowed.

quiz.q: A public mobile app needs sign-up and sign-in for 50,000 users, including sign-in with Google. Which service?
o: Amazon Cognito user pools
Right. Cognito handles app users, social sign-in and tokens at scale.
IAM users
IAM users are for people and code working on your AWS account, not app customers.
IAM Identity Center
Identity Center is for your workforce signing in to AWS accounts and business apps.
AWS Directory Service
That runs Active Directory. It isn't built for public app sign-up.

quiz.q: Rules say S3 data must be encrypted at rest with a key your unit controls, every use of the key logged in CloudTrail, and the key rotated. What meets this with the LEAST effort?
o: SSE-KMS with a customer managed key and automatic rotation turned on
Right. You control the key policy, KMS logs every use to CloudTrail, and rotation is a checkbox.
SSE-S3
AWS owns and manages those keys. You can't control or audit them per key.
SSE-C with keys supplied on every request
AWS doesn't keep the key, so your app must send it every time. That's a lot more effort.
Client-side encryption with keys kept on an admin's laptop
More work and much riskier. There's no central control or logging.

quiz.q: The Organizations admin must make sure nobody in any member account can stop or delete CloudTrail, including account admins. What should they use?
o: An SCP that denies cloudtrail:StopLogging and cloudtrail:DeleteTrail, attached to the OU
Right. An SCP deny applies to everyone in those accounts, admins included, and they can't remove it.
An IAM policy that denies those actions, attached to each admin
Admins can edit or remove their own policies.
An AWS Config rule that checks CloudTrail is on
Config detects the change after it happens. It doesn't prevent it.
A permissions boundary on every new role
Boundaries apply per user or role, and a local admin could change them.

quiz.q: A web tier sends orders straight to a processing tier. During sales the processors fall behind and orders are lost. What fixes this with the LEAST change?
o: Put an SQS queue between the tiers and scale processors on queue depth
Right. The queue holds every order until a processor is free, so nothing is lost in a spike.
Move the processing tier to a bigger instance
It raises the ceiling, but a big enough spike still loses orders.
Use an SNS topic between the tiers
SNS pushes messages right away. It doesn't hold them for slow consumers.
Use Kinesis Data Streams with one shard
More complex, and one shard caps throughput. A queue is the simple fit.

quiz.q: An RDS MySQL database must survive the loss of an Availability Zone with automatic failover and no data loss. What should you use?
o: A Multi-AZ deployment
Right. Multi-AZ keeps a synchronous standby in another AZ and fails over automatically.
A read replica in another AZ
Replication is asynchronous, so recent writes can be lost, and promoting it isn't automatic failover.
Daily snapshots copied to another Region
Restoring takes time and you lose up to a day of data.
A larger instance class
Still a single instance in a single AZ.

quiz.q: After a Region outage, an app must be back within minutes. A smaller copy of the whole stack may run all the time, but a full-size second Region is too expensive. Which DR strategy?
o: Warm standby
Right. A scaled-down but fully working copy runs all the time and scales up when you fail over.
Pilot light
Only the data layer runs. Servers must start first, so recovery takes longer.
Backup and restore
Rebuilding from backups takes hours.
Multi-site active/active
That's the full-size second Region they said is too expensive.

quiz.q: A training site must switch to a backup copy in another Region automatically when the primary fails its health checks. Which Route 53 routing policy?
o: Failover routing with health checks
Right. Traffic goes to the primary and moves to the secondary only when the primary is unhealthy.
Weighted routing, 50/50
That splits traffic between both all the time.
Geolocation routing
It routes by where users are, not by whether a site is healthy.
Simple routing with both IP addresses
Simple routing can't use health checks, so users may still get the failed site.

quiz.q: Two hundred Windows servers need a shared file share that uses SMB and is joined to Active Directory. Which service?
o: Amazon FSx for Windows File Server
Right. It's a managed Windows file system with SMB and AD.
Amazon EFS
EFS uses NFS for Linux. It isn't a Windows SMB share.
Amazon FSx for Lustre
Lustre is a high-performance Linux file system for compute jobs.
Amazon EBS
A block volume for EC2, not a shared file share.

quiz.q: A read-heavy app keeps running the same queries, and RDS CPU is high. Reads need sub-millisecond latency and can be a few seconds stale. What's the BEST fix?
o: Add Amazon ElastiCache in front of the database
Right. An in-memory cache answers repeated reads in microseconds and takes load off RDS.
Turn on Multi-AZ
A standard Multi-AZ standby doesn't serve reads. It's for failover.
Move to a larger DB instance
More CPU helps, but reads still come from the database in milliseconds, at a higher cost.
Add DynamoDB Accelerator (DAX)
DAX only caches DynamoDB, not RDS.

quiz.q: Users around the world upload large files to an S3 bucket in us-east-1 and say uploads are slow. What helps MOST with the least change?
o: Turn on S3 Transfer Acceleration
Right. Uploads enter AWS at the nearest edge location and ride AWS's network to the bucket.
Turn on Cross-Region Replication
It copies objects after they arrive. It doesn't speed up the upload.
Move the bucket to a bigger storage class
Storage classes change cost and retrieval, not upload speed.
Put a NAT gateway in front of the bucket
NAT gateways are for private subnets reaching out, not for users uploading.

quiz.q: Logs are read often for 30 days, rarely for the rest of the year, then must be kept 7 years for legal reasons but almost never read. What's MOST cost-effective?
o: A lifecycle rule: Standard, to Standard-IA at 30 days, to Glacier Deep Archive at 365 days, then expire at 7 years
Right. Each step matches the access pattern, and expiring at 7 years stops paying for data you no longer need.
Keep everything in S3 Standard
Simple, but you'd pay top price for years of data nobody reads.
Put everything in S3 One Zone-IA on day one
One AZ is less durable, and early, frequent reads cost more in IA classes.
Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering and keep the logs forever
It works for unknown patterns, but this pattern is known, and keeping them forever costs more.

quiz.q: A steady fleet runs all year. Midyear the team may switch from general-purpose to compute-optimized instances. Which pricing option saves the most and allows that change?
o: A Compute Savings Plan
Right. It applies across instance families, sizes and Regions, and to Fargate and Lambda too.
Standard Reserved Instances
Standard RIs are tied to an instance family. You can't switch families.
Spot Instances
Steady production work shouldn't depend on capacity that can be taken back.
On-Demand
Flexible, but the most expensive option for a steady fleet.

quiz.q: NAT gateway data charges are high. Most traffic is private EC2 instances reading from S3 and DynamoDB in the same Region. What cuts the cost MOST?
o: Add gateway VPC endpoints for S3 and DynamoDB
Right. Gateway endpoints have no hourly or per-GB charge and keep the traffic off the NAT gateway.
Move the instances to public subnets with public IPs
It removes the NAT charge but exposes the instances to the internet.
Add a second NAT gateway
That adds cost. It doesn't lower it.
Add interface endpoints for both services
They work, but interface endpoints charge per hour and per GB. Gateway endpoints are free.

pbqs.title: Fix the architecture
pbqs.scenario: A design review found six problems in your unit's AWS app. Pick the change that fixes each one. Each fix is used once; two are distractors.

rows.req: The web tier is one EC2 instance. When it fails, the site is down.
rows.why: A load balancer across AZs plus Auto Scaling replaces failed instances and spreads load.

rows.req: The database is one RDS instance in one AZ.
rows.why: Multi-AZ adds a synchronous standby in another AZ with automatic failover.

rows.req: Orders are lost when the processing tier falls behind.
rows.why: A queue holds orders until a worker is free.

rows.req: Pictures load slowly for users in Europe and Asia.
rows.why: CloudFront caches content at edge locations near users.

rows.req: Private instances reach S3 through an expensive NAT gateway.
rows.why: A gateway endpoint sends S3 traffic privately at no extra charge.

rows.req: Years of old logs sit in S3 Standard.
rows.why: A lifecycle rule moves old data to cheaper classes and deletes it on schedule.

pbqs.title: Pick the recovery strategy
pbqs.scenario: Five systems need a recovery plan. Pick the cheapest strategy that still meets each requirement. One choice is a distractor.

items.text: Can be down for a day. Losing a day of changes is fine. Cheapest possible.
items.why: Backups copied to another Region are the cheapest, and hours of downtime are acceptable.

items.text: The database must replicate all the time, but app servers can stay off until needed. Back within about an hour.
items.why: Pilot light keeps only the core data running and starts the rest during recovery.

items.text: Must be back within minutes. A smaller full copy may run all the time.
items.why: Warm standby runs a scaled-down working copy ready to scale up.

items.text: No downtime allowed, even if a whole Region fails. Both Regions serve users.
items.why: Only active/active in two Regions gives near-zero downtime for a Region failure.

items.text: Must survive one data center failing. A Region-wide outage is an accepted risk.
items.why: Spreading across AZs in one Region handles a data center failure without paying for a second Region.

pbqs.title: Pick the database
pbqs.scenario: Six teams are choosing databases. Pick the best fit for each. Each choice is used once; one is a distractor.

rows.req: A relational order system with steady load that needs automatic failover
rows.why: RDS with Multi-AZ is the standard choice for steady relational workloads that must fail over.

rows.req: A relational app used a few hours a week with unpredictable spikes
rows.why: Aurora Serverless scales capacity with demand, so you don't pay for idle hours.

rows.req: A shopping cart for millions of users with millisecond reads at any scale
rows.why: DynamoDB is serverless key-value storage built for that scale.

rows.req: A session store that needs microsecond reads
rows.why: ElastiCache keeps data in memory for the fastest reads.

rows.req: Analysts run SQL over years of sales data
rows.why: Redshift is the data warehouse for analytics on large data sets.

rows.req: Find “friends of friends” and other relationship queries
rows.why: Neptune is a graph database built for relationships.
